JSON: Name: transvfc_pipeline Title: Transformable video feature compression framework for scalable machine-vision downstream tasks Short Hypothesis: A compress-then-transfer pipeline combining a scheme-based inter-prediction video feature codec with perception-guided conditional coding and lightweight task-specific feature-space transforms causes a statistically significant reduction in bitrate required to achieve equivalent downstream task performance (AP or mIoU) compared to conventional pixel-domain codecs and existing feature-compression approaches. Related Work: Prior work splits into pixel-domain codecs optimized for human perception and neural video compression (NVC) approaches that focus on pixel reconstruction. Analyze-then-compress (ATC) methods compress intermediate features to reduce transmitted data for machine tasks, but most existing ATC solutions address only intra-frame redundancy and either require task-specific codec optimization or fine-tuning of downstream networks. Neural video compression methods reduce temporal redundancy but operate in the pixel domain or use feature-domain motion compensation via deformable convolution; these methods either do not exploit explicit perception priors or incur high computational cost. Recent VCM efforts that jointly optimize codec and a single downstream task show good task performance but lack scalability across tasks because they require retraining upstream or downstream models. Remaining limitations include inadequate temporal redundancy modeling in feature space, lack of a modular transfer layer to map reconstructed features to multiple task backbones, and high compute/latency for high-performance NVC models. Abstract: This work addresses efficient video transmission for machine-centric downstream tasks by proposing a transformable video feature compression pipeline. The pipeline comprises a neural video feature codec that reduces temporal redundancy via a scheme-based inter-prediction stage and removes spatial residuals with perception-guided conditional coding, and a set of lightweight feature-space transform (FST) modules that map reconstructed intermediate features to task-specific feature spaces. Only the appropriate FST needs to be trained when adding a new downstream task, preserving the upstream codec and downstream backbones unchanged. The principal contribution is a compress-then-transfer architecture that jointly (1) squeezes temporal and spatial redundancy in feature space using explicit motion scheme generation and perception priors, and (2) provides scalable per-task adapters that enable reuse of a single transmitted feature stream for multiple analysis networks. Expected outcomes are lower bitrates to reach target task metrics, reduced re-training/deployment overhead when supporting new tasks, and practical encoder/decoder complexity for machine-vision pipelines. Experiments: Datasets: YouTube-VIS2019 for video instance segmentation; VSPW for video semantic segmentation; a video detection subset derived from ImageNet VID or COCO-VID for object detection (matching report splits). Downstream backbones: CrossVIS (ResNet50) for instance segmentation, DeepLab-v3 (ResNet50) for semantic segmentation, Faster R-CNN (ResNet50) for object detection. Baselines: VTM-23.1 (pixel codec anchor), HM-18.0, x265 (FFmpeg), SMC++, FVC, DCVC, DCVC-TCM, DCVC-HEM, DCVC-DC; plus ATC variants that (a) fine-tune upstream codec for each task and (b) fine-tune downstream networks while freezing codec. Metrics: bits-per-pixel (bpp), AP (object detection & instance segmentation), mIoU (semantic segmentation), PSNR and MS-SSIM of reconstructed frames, BD-Rate relative to VTM for rate-task curves, encoding and decoding latency (ms) measured on NVIDIA RTX3090, model parameter counts and MACs per pixel, and statistical significance (paired t-test, p<0.05) on rate-task results. Implementation / Training: two-stage optimization—stage 1 train video feature codec on YouTube-VIS2019-train with multiple rate points (λ settings corresponding to target bpp values); stage 2 freeze codec and train per-task FSTs on task-specific train splits for 100k iterations at lr=1e-5. Evaluation: generate rate-task curves by sweeping bitrate points for all methods, compute BD-Rate against VTM, and report latency/perf tradeoffs. Ablations: (A) remove scheme-based inter-prediction and replace with deformable-convolution compensation; (B) train codec without perception-guided conditional coding (remove conditions); (C) remove perception loss term from codec objective; (D) ablate FST branches (remove up-then-down, down-then-up, bottleneck) and measure BD-Rate and downstream metrics; (E) compare three ATC deployment modes: only FST training (proposed), fine-tune upstream codec per task, fine-tune downstream backbones per task—report additional params, GPU memory, and training time per step. Robustness tests: evaluate on corrupted inputs: low-light simulated (reduce Y channel by 0.3) and additive Gaussian noise (σ=25); report rate-task curves and BD-Rate changes. Success criterion: proposed pipeline achieves negative BD-Rate (bitrate reduction) with no statistically significant drop in downstream performance versus VTM and outperforms baselines in at least two downstream tasks. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Accumulated temporal error: scheme-based inter-prediction can propagate mis-compensation across frames, causing degraded reconstructed features at low bitrates. 2) Sensitivity to pixel-domain noise: feature extraction from noisy or corrupted frames can reduce compression efficiency and task performance. 3) Domain/generalization limits: networks and perception priors trained on specific datasets may not generalize to other scenes, resolutions, or sensor types. 4) Scalability constraints: although FST modules are lightweight, supporting many simultaneous tasks increases overall server-side memory and per-task decoder workload. 5) Latency and real-time limits: entropy coding and decoder-side perception conditioning add runtime; meeting strict real-time constraints on edge devices may be infeasible. 6) Dependence on frozen perception network: using fixed perception conditions constrains codec adaptability to novel downstream architectures that provide divergent internal features. 7) Evaluation bias: reported gains may be dataset- and backbone-dependent; BD-Rate computed against a single anchor (VTM) may not reflect all operational deployments. 8) Compute and training resources: two-stage training and per-task FST training still require GPU resources that may limit on-device or low-resource deployment.
